title: Ezekiel 29:17–21
context: Ezekiel 29:17–21 is dated to the twenty-seventh year, first month, first day, often placed around 571 BC. It appears to be the latest dated oracle in the book, and it is placed here with the other words about Egypt rather than in date order. The LORD tells the prophet that Nebuchadnezzar and his army labored hard against Tyre until every head was rubbed bald and every shoulder worn, yet they received no wages from Tyre. So the LORD will give Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar as payment for his army, because they worked for him. Earlier, in 26:7–14, the prophet announced Nebuchadnezzar’s attack on Tyre and its destruction. This later word sets the outcome at Tyre beside a new word about Egypt, and readers explain the relationship between the two passages in different ways. The text itself places them side by side without explanation. The unit ends with a promise that the LORD will make a horn sprout for Israel and open the prophet’s mouth among them.

verses.text: It came to pass in the twenty-seventh year, in the first month, in the first day of the month, the LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet reports a word dated to the twenty-seventh year, first month, first day. Arminian readers see that this oracle comes many years after the others in the collection, which shows that Ezekiel’s ministry continued long after Jerusalem fell.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that this appears to be the latest dated oracle in the book. Both traditions hold the modern date loosely, often placing it around 571 BC, and note that it is placed here by topic rather than in date order.

verses.text: “Son of man, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon caused his army to serve a great service against Tyre. Every head was made bald, and every shoulder was worn; yet he had no wages, nor did his army, from Tyre, for the service that he had served against it.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says Nebuchadnezzar’s army labored hard against Tyre until heads were bald and shoulders worn, yet got no wages from Tyre. Arminians see an honest account of how events at Tyre turned out for the Babylonian army.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the verse as stating plainly what happened at Tyre. Both traditions note that 26:7–14 announced Nebuchadnezzar’s attack on Tyre, and they name the relationship between the two passages without forcing a single explanation.

verses.text: Therefore the Lord GOD says: ‘Behold, I will give the land of Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon. He will carry off her multitude, take her plunder, and take her prey. That will be the wages for his army.
verses.arminianNotes: The Lord GOD says he will give Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar, who will take its wealth as wages for his army. Arminian readers see God directing the course of history, giving one nation into another’s hand.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereign disposal of the nations. Both traditions note that Jeremiah 43:8–13 and 46:13–26 also speak of Nebuchadnezzar coming against Egypt, and they name these without harmonizing details.

verses.text: I have given him the land of Egypt as his payment for which he served, because they worked for me,’ says the Lord GOD.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he has given Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar as payment, because they worked for him. Arminians see God using even a pagan king for his purposes, while that king remains responsible for his own actions.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereignty over the plans of rulers. Both traditions note that how God uses Babylon as his instrument is discussed at the Judges 9:23 box.

verses.text: “In that day I will cause a horn to sprout for the house of Israel, and I will open your mouth among them. Then they will know that I am the LORD.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says that in that day he will make a horn sprout for Israel and open the prophet’s mouth among them. Arminian readers see hope for Israel, as the horn is a common image of strength and restored power.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the horn as a sign of God’s renewed favor (compare Psalm 132:17). Both traditions note that the opening of the prophet’s mouth may connect with 24:27 and 33:22, and they read the verse as hope after judgment.
